mbielu-mbielu-mbielu|Roy Mackal's expedi.summary: During his 1980 trip to the Likouala region, University of Chicago biologist Roy Mackal gathered local descriptions of an animal with 'planks' growing from its back. One informant picked a Stegosaurus picture from his books, but said she had only heard of it from older relatives. Mackal himself thought it might be a large monitor lizard and called it an enigma; no evidence has been found.

melon-heads|Melonheads film.summary: The Michigan version of the melon heads legend, about deformed children said to roam the woods near the Felt Mansion in Ottawa County, inspired a 2011 low-budget film called The Melonheads. It is one of several films based on the regional legends, which have no documented basis.

memphre|Dracontology society founded.summary: Diver Jacques Boisvert, who said he made over 1,000 dives in Lake Memphremagog without finding proof of a creature, founded the International Dracontology Society on June 19, 1986 to collect and study sightings. He coined 'dracontology' for the study of lake and sea serpents; by 2000 the society had logged over 200 reported sightings.
memphre|Dracontology society founded.source_title: Welcome to Ogopogo Country - Canada's Lake Creature (Memphré, Library and Archives Canada archive)

memphre|Royal Canadian Mint coloured qua.summary: In August 2011 the Royal Canadian Mint issued a coloured 25-cent coin featuring an artist's impression of Memphré, the creature said to live in Lake Memphremagog.

men-in-black|Maury Island warning.summary: Harbor patrolman Harold Dahl claimed that on June 21, 1947 he saw six doughnut-shaped craft over Maury Island, one dropping debris, and that a man in a dark suit later warned him not to talk about it. It is often cited as the first 'men in black' story. The whole incident is widely regarded as a hoax; Project Blue Book's Edward Ruppelt called it 'the dirtiest hoax in UFO history'.

men-in-black|Albert K. Bender visit.summary: Albert K. Bender, who ran the International Flying Saucer Bureau from Bridgeport, said that in 1953 three men dressed in black visited him and frightened him out of publishing his UFO findings. He shut down the bureau soon after. Gray Barker's book about the episode launched the men in black legend; some writers suspect Bender's experience was a dream.

men-in-black|Point Pleasant visits.summary: During the 1966-67 Mothman flap, writer John Keel claimed that Point Pleasant residents received visits from strange, threatening men in black, alongside UFO sightings and premonitions. He described these in The Mothman Prophecies (1975). Keel also admitted that some MIB stories had mundane causes, recounting a night in 1967 when he himself was mistaken for one.

menehune|Census of Kauaʻi lists 65 peopl.summary: An 1820 census of Kauaʻi taken under the island's ruling chief Kaumualiʻi is said to have listed 65 people as menehune. Some early scholars read this as evidence that 'menehune' was a term for a social class of commoners rather than a race of small people, though that theory is debated.

menehune|ʻAlekoko (Menehune) Fishpond li.summary: The ʻAlekoko Fishpond near Līhuʻe, a 900-foot stone-walled fishpond on the Hulēʻia River, was listed on the U.S. National Register of Historic Places in 1973. Hawaiian tradition credits its construction to the Menehune; it is thought to date from about the 15th century and is now being restored by the nonprofit Mālama Hulēʻia.

mermaid|Columbus sees three 'sirens', al.summary: In January 1493, sailing off Hispaniola, Christopher Columbus wrote that he saw three 'sirens' rise out of the sea and that they were not as beautiful as they are painted. Historians widely believe he saw manatees.

mermaid|The Benbecula mermaid is said to.summary: A local story from the Outer Hebrides says a small mermaid-like creature was found on Benbecula around 1830 and buried near the sea. The tale survives only as local legend; no remains have been documented.

mermaid|P. T. Barnum shows the 'Feejee m.summary: In 1842 showman P. T. Barnum exhibited the 'Feejee mermaid' in New York, drumming up interest with fake letters and a fake naturalist, 'Dr. J. Griffin'. The object was a monkey's head and torso sewn onto a fish tail. The original later disappeared, probably in one of the fires at Barnum's museum.

mermaid|Town offers $1 million for proof.summary: In August 2009, after dozens of people said they saw a mermaid leaping from the water off Kiryat Yam in Haifa Bay, the town offered a $1 million reward for proof that it existed. The offer drew wide media coverage, but no proof was produced.

mermaid|Dam workers refuse to work, blam.summary: In February 2012, work on reservoirs near Gokwe and Mutare in Zimbabwe stopped when workers refused to continue, saying mermaids (in local tradition, water spirits) had driven them away. The case was reported by water resources minister Samuel Sipepa Nkomo.

mermaid|Osborne Dam reports reach Zimbab.summary: In February 2012 water resources minister Sam Sipepa Nkomo told a Senate committee that workers at the Osborne Dam in Manicaland and at Gokwe were refusing to return, saying mermaids had chased them off, and that traditional rituals would be held before repairs. He said he did not personally believe in mermaids and suggested strong currents might explain the danger.
mermaid|Osborne Dam reports reach Zimbab.source_title: 'Mermaid' Sightings in Zimbabwe Spark Debate Over Traditional Beliefs - VOA Zimbabwe

minhocao|Fritz Müller publishes highland.summary: In 1878 German naturalist Fritz Müller published reports from southern Brazil's highlands, largely from a resident of Curitibanos, describing a giant burrowing worm-like creature that uprooted trees and left trenches. Nature summarised the accounts. Müller suggested a giant lungfish; scientists were sceptical and no specimen was ever produced.

minnesota-iceman|Sanderson and Heuvelman.summary: In December 1968 zoologists Ivan T. Sanderson and Bernard Heuvelmans examined the frozen 'Iceman' at exhibitor Frank Hansen's home in Minnesota. Both became convinced it was a real hairy hominid, and Heuvelmans named it Homo pongoides in 1969. The Smithsonian's John Napier later concluded it was a latex carnival model, and it is now widely regarded as a hoax.
minnesota-iceman|Sanderson and Heuvelman.source_title: The Strange Case of the Minnesota Iceman - Scientific American

minnesota-iceman|Argosy \"missing link\".summary: Ivan T. Sanderson, science editor of Argosy, wrote about the Iceman in the April 1969 issue under the headline 'Is this the missing link between man and the apes?'. When the Smithsonian's John Napier looked into it, exhibitor Frank Hansen withdrew it, and Napier concluded it was a latex-and-hair carnival model.

minnesota-iceman|Sold on eBay to the Mus.summary: In February 2013 the Iceman was listed on eBay as 'the actual sideshow gaff' and 'a one of a kind hoax'. It was bought by Steve Busti, owner of the Museum of the Weird in Austin, Texas, where it is on display.

mngwa|Hichens' Discovery article.summary: British colonial officer William Hichens, who served in Tanganyika, wrote in the late 1930s about villagers' accounts of the mngwa or nunda, a huge cat said to attack people at night, and of paw prints larger than any known big cat. Hichens himself thought an unusually large lion was the likelier culprit. No specimen has ever been found.

moca-vampire|Drained livestock found in.summary: On February 25, 1975, newspapers reported that fifteen cows, three goats, two geese and a pig had been found in Moca with puncture wounds and drained of blood. Residents linked the deaths to UFO sightings, and similar reports followed elsewhere in Puerto Rico that year. The 'Vampiro de Moca' is seen as a forerunner of the chupacabra legend; no cause was confirmed.

moddey-dhoo|George Waldron's description.summary: English writer George Waldron's description of the Isle of Man, published in 1731, recorded the 'Mauthe Doog', a black spectral dog said to haunt Peel Castle. He told of a drunken guard who defied it, came back speechless with terror and died three days later. Sir Walter Scott later used the story in Peveril of the Peak (1823).

moddey-dhoo|Doctor meets a calf-sized bl.summary: Manx folklore collector W. W. Gill recorded that in 1931 a doctor driving past Milntown corner near Ramsey met 'a big black dog-like creature nearly the size of a calf, with bright staring eyes'. A similar sighting at the same spot had been reported in 1927. The accounts are folklore records only.

mogollon-monster|Grand Canyon wild man s.summary: In 1903 The Arizona Republican printed I. W. Stevens's account of a wild man near the Grand Canyon with long white hair, a knee-length beard and two-inch claws, which he said he found drinking the blood of two cougars before it threatened him with a club. It is the oldest known report linked to the Mogollon Monster and is unverified.

mogollon-monster|Don Davis scout-trip si.summary: Cryptozoologist Don Davis said that in the mid-1940s, on a Boy Scout trip near Payson, he saw a huge creature with deep-set eyes, a square head and massive arms. His account is one of the best-known Mogollon Monster reports; it rests on his recollection alone.

mokele-mbembe|Lake Tele expeditions.summary: In 1980 and 1981 biologist Roy Mackal and explorer Powell travelled to the Likouala region of the Congo to interview residents about mokele-mbembe. They found no physical evidence but argued the consistent accounts supported its existence. Critics say they accepted testimony uncritically; later expeditions also found nothing, and many researchers trace the legend to rhinoceros folk memory.

momo|Momo flap.summary: On July 11, 1972, children playing outside a home on the edge of Louisiana, Missouri screamed, and their older sister said she saw a huge, dark-haired, man-like creature holding what looked like a dead dog. Its head was described as 'pumpkin-shaped'. More reports followed that year, including one from the local fire chief, and a 20-person posse searched without success.

mongolian-death-worm|Roy Chapman Andrews.summary: American explorer Roy Chapman Andrews introduced the olgoi-khorkhoi to Western readers in his 1926 book On the Trail of Ancient Man. He recorded second-hand descriptions given by Mongolian officials, including the prime minister, though none had seen it themselves. Andrews did not believe it existed.

monkey-man-of-delhi|Monkey-man panic swe.summary: In May 2001, reports spread in New Delhi of a monkey-like creature attacking people at night. Descriptions varied wildly, from a four-foot hairy figure with a metal helmet and claws to an eight-foot creature leaping between buildings. Police logged over 350 reports, and two or three people died falling in panic; the episode is generally described as mass hysteria.

montauk-monster|Carcass found at Ditch P.summary: In July 2008 a strange, hairless carcass with a beak-like face washed up at Ditch Plains beach in Montauk, and a local newspaper ran the photo as 'The Hound of Bonacville'. Theories ranged from a turtle to a Plum Island experiment. Experts including palaeozoologist Darren Naish concluded it was a decomposed raccoon.

morag|Earliest recorded sighting.summary: Reported sightings of a creature in Loch Morar date back to 1887. By 1981 researchers had logged 34 incidents, sixteen of them with more than one witness. None has produced physical evidence.

morag|McDonell and Simpson boat encounte.summary: In August 1969 Duncan McDonell and William Simpson said their boat struck a creature in Loch Morar, which then came at them. McDonell fended it off with an oar and Simpson fired a rifle before it sank from view. They described it as brown, 25-30 ft long with rough skin; the claim was widely reported but never confirmed.

morgawr|'Mary F' photographs sent to the.summary: In 1976 the Falmouth Packet received photos of a humped sea serpent in Falmouth Bay, sent by someone signing only as 'Mary F'. Folklorists believe Cornish showman Tony 'Doc' Shiels was behind them; a 2022 academic article argues the whole Morgawr story began as a hoax.

morgawr|Two fishermen report the creatur.summary: In July 1976 two fishermen said they saw the creature in the sea off Lizard Point, Cornwall. The report came in the same year as the 'Mary F' photos, during a flurry of claims that folklorists link to a hoax.

mothman|TNT area chase.summary: On November 15, 1966, two young couples driving near the former WWII TNT plant outside Point Pleasant told police that a tall winged figure with glowing red eyes followed their car at high speed. Dozens of similar reports followed. A West Virginia University wildlife biologist suggested a sandhill crane; others blame owls or herons.

mothman|Silver Bridge collapse.summary: On December 15, 1967 the Silver Bridge between Point Pleasant and Ohio collapsed at rush hour, killing 46 people. Engineers traced it to a failed eyebar in the suspension chain. Writers such as John Keel later tied the Mothman sightings to the disaster, creating the legend that Mothman was an omen.

mussie|First anecdotes of the lake creat.summary: Stories of a large unknown animal in Muskrat Lake near Cobden date back to about 1916, when it was called 'Hapyxelor'. A claim that Samuel de Champlain wrote about it has never been backed up. The creature, later nicknamed Mussie, is now a local tourism mascot; no evidence has been found.

mystery-airships|Sacramento sightings.summary: On November 17, 1896 a moving light crossed the night sky over Sacramento, seen by hundreds of people; a few said they saw a dark shape behind it. It returned on November 21 and was reported across the Bay Area. Newspapers ran wild stories about a secret inventor's airship, starting the 1896-97 airship wave; no airship was ever found.

mystery-airships|Aurora crash story.summary: The Dallas Morning News of April 19, 1897 reported that an airship had hit a windmill in Aurora, Texas and crashed, and that its pilot, 'not an inhabitant of this world', was buried in the town cemetery. No other papers reported the funeral. UFO fans revived the tale in the 1960s, but by the 1970s most researchers considered it a hoax.

mystery-airships|Cow-napping airship tal.summary: Alexander Hamilton of Le Roy, Kansas claimed in April 1897 that an airship lassoed a heifer from his pen and flew off with it. The story ran in the Yates Center Farmer's Advocate. In 1977 researcher Jerome Clark showed it was a tall tale written to win a local Liars' Club contest.

nahuelito|Garret sighting.summary: George Garret, who worked near Nahuel Huapi Lake, said that in 1910 he saw a creature about 400 m away, its visible part 5-7 m long and 2 m out of the water. He only made it public in 1922 in a letter to a Toronto newspaper, which helped spark a search for the creature.

nahuelito|Onelli plesiosaur expedition.summary: In 1922 Clemente Onelli, director of the Buenos Aires Zoo, backed an expedition to look for a 'plesiosaur' in a Patagonian lake after reports including George Garret's. The search found no evidence, though the small lake involved is still called Laguna del Plesiosaurio.

nahuelito|Anonymous hump photos.summary: In 1988 a magazine of the Río Negro newspaper published photos of a hump in the water near the Bariloche shore. They came with a letter from a man who would not give his name, insisting it was not a log or a wave. The photos have never been verified.

nain-rouge|Seen after the Battle of Bloo.summary: Detroit legend says the Nain Rouge, a red imp, appeared before the Battle of Bloody Run on July 30, 1763, when Pontiac's forces killed about 58 British soldiers, and 'danced among the corpses' afterwards. The tale is folklore; the battle itself is a documented event of Pontiac's War.

nain-rouge|Sighting before the riots.summary: According to local lore, two utility workers said they saw the Nain Rouge shortly before the 1967 Detroit riots, keeping its reputation as a harbinger of disaster. The story is part of the legend and is unverified.

nain-rouge|First Marche du Nain Rouge.summary: Since 2010, Detroit has held the Marche du Nain Rouge each spring, a costumed parade in which someone dressed as the imp is chased out of the city and an effigy is burned to 'banish' it for another year. Marchers wear masks so the Nain Rouge won't recognise them.

nandi-bear|Hobley's footprint drawing.summary: In 1914 British colonial administrator Charles William Hobley published a drawing of a footprint attributed to the Nandi bear, a fierce animal described by people in western Kenya. It remains one of the few physical traces linked to the creature, and its source animal is unknown.

nandi-bear|Chalicothere theory proposed.summary: In 1923 palaeontologist Charles William Andrews suggested the Nandi bear could be a surviving chalicothere, an extinct clawed mammal; Louis Leakey later made a similar suggestion. The idea was dropped, as chalicotheres were herbivores. Many reports were instead put down to spotted hyenas or honey badgers.

ningen|Mu magazine article.summary: In late 2007 the Japanese paranormal magazine Mu ran an article on a white, human-shaped figure spotted on Google Earth off Namibia, linking it to the 'ningen' stories that had started on the 2channel forum. Skeptics suggest such images show icebergs or whales; the ningen is generally treated as modern internet folklore.

ningyo|A ningyo in Obama Bay is taken as.summary: Japanese records list a ningyo (fish-like 'mermaid') appearing in Obama Bay in Wakasa Province in 1310. Unlike many ningyo sightings, which were read as bad omens, this one was considered auspicious and was given the name 'True Immortal'.

ningyo|A 'white nun' said to be 800 year.summary: Fifteenth-century sources say a 'white nun' (Shira Bikuni) aged 800 appeared in Kyoto around 1449. She is linked to the legend of Yao Bikuni, a girl from Obama in Wakasa who gained near-endless youth by eating ningyo flesh. The tale is folklore.

ningyo|Enjuin temple's 'mermaid mummy' s.summary: Researchers from Kurashiki University of Science and the Arts studied a foot-long 'mermaid mummy' kept at Enju-in temple in Asakuchi. Their results, reported in February 2023, showed it was made of cloth, cotton and paper with fish skin and animal hair, with no real skeleton, and that it probably dated from the late 1800s.
ningyo|Enjuin temple's 'mermaid mummy' s.source_title: We Finally Know What Japan's Eerie Mummified Mer-Monkey Really Is - ScienceAlert

nittaewo|Army captain searches the Kudum.summary: In 1963 Sri Lankan army captain A. T. Rambukwella led a search of the caves at Kudumbigala for traces of the nittaewo, small hairy people of Vedda tradition. He reported finding mollusc shells and turtle remains, foods the nittaewo were said to eat, but no direct evidence of the creatures.

nordic-aliens|Adamski meets Orthon.summary: George Adamski claimed that on November 20, 1952, in the desert near Desert Center, California, he met Orthon, a long-haired, human-looking visitor from Venus who warned against nuclear weapons. His book Flying Saucers Have Landed became a bestseller. Investigators found that the companions he named contradicted his story, and he is widely regarded as a hoaxer.

nordic-aliens|Billy Meier contacts begin.summary: Swiss contactee Eduard 'Billy' Meier says that on January 28, 1975 he met Semjase, a woman from the 'Plejaren', starting a long series of claimed contacts. He produced many photos and films of 'beamships'. Scientists, skeptics and most ufologists consider them hoaxes, and Meier admitted to using models in some re-created scenes.

ogopogo|Folden film.summary: In 1968 Art Folden stopped on Highway 97 and filmed what he said was a large creature making a wake in Okanagan Lake. The footage became one of the best-known pieces of Ogopogo evidence. A 2005 re-analysis for National Geographic found the object was much closer and smaller than claimed, probably a bird, otter or beaver.

old-ned|Schooner crew reports a sea serp.summary: On July 28, 1908 the crew of the schooner Madagasca reported seeing a sea serpent in the Bay of Fundy near Cutler, Maine. Local lore links the report to Old Ned, the creature said to live in nearby Lake Utopia, New Brunswick. Nothing was ever confirmed.

old-yellow-top|First reported sighting.summary: Local legend says a Sasquatch-like creature with a light-coloured mane and a visible limp was first seen around the mines of Cobalt, Ontario in 1906. Residents nicknamed it 'Old Yellow Top'. The story comes from old local newspaper reports and has never been verified.
old-yellow-top|First reported sighting.source_title: New film will try to find Sasquatch in Northern Ontario - Cottage Life

old-yellow-top|Blueberry patch encounter.note: Could not find a reliable source. Only a fringe wiki (Kook Science, 'Old Yellow Top') and a blog describe it: two prospectors near the Wettlaufer Mine, Cobalt, said they saw a bear-like animal with a yellowish head in a blueberry patch (July 1923), reportedly printed in the North Bay Nugget. Needs a newspaper archive check before publishing.

orang-pendek|Debbie Martyr's sightings.summary: British conservationist Debbie Martyr, who spent years researching in Kerinci Seblat National Park, reported seeing an orang pendek three times, twice in July 1989 and again on September 30, 1994, when she watched an upright creature cross a valley about 30 m away. Later searches have produced disputed footprint casts but no conclusive proof.
orang-pendek|Debbie Martyr's sightings.source_title: Apakah Orang Pendek di Hutan Sumatera Ada? - Mongabay Indonesia

owlman|Mawnan church sighting.summary: In April 1976 two young sisters on holiday reportedly saw a large feathered 'bird-man' hovering over the tower of Mawnan church, and their father cut the holiday short. The story came through showman Tony 'Doc' Shiels, who named it the Owlman; later witnesses also reported only to him. Many suspect a hoax by Shiels or a misidentified barn owl.

ozark-howler|Wildlife emergency call nea.summary: In October 2014 the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission logged an emergency call from a motorist who nearly hit an unidentified, bear-sized, grey, fast-running animal on Pump Station Road in Springdale. Wildlife officers may have been sent to look; no animal was identified.

ozark-howler|Photo hoax sent to TV stati.summary: In December 2015 Arkansas station 40/29 News received photos from a viewer said to show the Ozark Howler. The station asked the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission, which said it had no reports of the creature and that the images were a hoax.

piasa|Marquette and Jolliet see the pain.summary: In 1673, travelling down the Mississippi, French explorers Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet described two large painted monsters on the bluffs near present-day Alton: human-faced, scaled creatures with long tails. The original paintings were destroyed by quarrying in the 1800s. Scholars link them to the underwater panther of regional Native traditions.

pixies|Coleridge visits the Pixies' Parl.summary: During his 1793 summer holiday in his hometown of Ottery St Mary, Devon, the young Samuel Taylor Coleridge led a party to the Pixies' Parlour, a small cave near the town, and wrote the poem 'Songs of the Pixies' about it. The town's Pixie Day tradition is tied to the same local lore.

pixies|Earliest Three Little Pigs tale,.summary: The earliest known printed version of 'The Three Little Pigs', published in 1853, comes from Dartmoor in Devon and features three little pixies and a fox instead of pigs and a wolf. The pig version became standard after James Halliwell-Phillipps and Joseph Jacobs printed it later in the century.

pope-lick-monster|Short film The Legend.summary: Louisville filmmaker Ron Schildknecht's 16-minute film The Legend of the Pope Lick Monster premiered on December 29, 1988. Norfolk Southern railway officials objected that it would lure teenagers onto the high trestle, and a safety warning was read at the premiere. Several people have since died on the trestle, some while looking for the monster.

popobawa|First reports on Pemba.summary: According to anthropological research, the first reports of the Popobawa, a night-time spirit said to assault sleepers, came from Pemba Island in 1965, shortly after the Zanzibar Revolution. Further scares followed in 1970 and the 1980s. Researchers link the attacks to sleep paralysis and to political anxiety.

popobawa|Great panic.summary: In 1995 fear of the Popobawa spread from Pemba to Unguja and on to Dar es Salaam and other coastal towns. Many people slept outdoors around fires to avoid being 'visited'. Skeptic Joe Nickell and others compared the reports to sleep paralysis, and the panic is usually described as mass hysteria.

popobawa|Renewed outbreak.summary: In February 2007 the BBC reported that men in parts of Dar es Salaam were afraid of a night-time sex attacker said to be the Popobawa, with some sleeping outside or in groups. The BBC's local correspondent noted that few people really believed in it and there had been no sightings.
popobawa|Renewed outbreak.source_title: Sex attacks blamed on bat demon - BBC News

puca|First Púca Festival held for Hallow.summary: Fáilte Ireland launched Púca as a new festival to promote Ireland as the home of Halloween, with its Samhain roots, first held from October 31 to November 2, 2019 around Trim, Athboy and Drogheda. It is named after the púca, a shape-shifting creature of Irish folklore linked to Samhain, and has returned in later years.
puca|First Púca Festival held for Hallow.source_title: Scary times ahead as the Púca heads for Athboy, Trim and Drogheda - Meath Chronicle

pukwudgie|Schoolcraft's Ojibwe stories.summary: In 1839 Henry Rowe Schoolcraft, whose wife Jane was of Ojibwe descent, published Algic Researches, including the story 'Puck Wudj Ininee' about the origin of the little people. It is the main early written source on the Pukwudgie, which is part of living Ojibwe and Wampanoag tradition.

pukwudgie|Longfellow's Song of Hiawatha.summary: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's 1855 poem The Song of Hiawatha, drawing on Schoolcraft's work, has the Pukwudgies kill the strong man Kwasind by pelting him with pine cones. The poem's popularity spread the name nationally, and stories of Pukwudgies were later relocated to Massachusetts.

queensland-tiger|Carl Lumholtz's Among C.summary: Norwegian naturalist Carl Lumholtz, who spent four years in Queensland including the Herbert River area, wrote in Among Cannibals (1889) that Aboriginal people described the yarri, a dingo-sized, savage, long-tailed animal that climbed trees when chased. He thought it might be an unknown 'marsupial tiger'. Its identity remains unknown.

redcap|Ballad of Lord Soulis and his red.summary: Walter Scott's Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border (1802) printed John Leyden's ballad 'Lord Soulis', in which the wicked lord of Hermitage Castle has a redcap familiar that protects him from weapons. Scott noted that ruined Border towers were each believed to house such a spirit. The real William de Soulis died in prison after a 1320 plot.

reptilians|Herbert Schirmer encounter.summary: Ashland police officer Herbert Schirmer reported in late 1967 that a saucer-shaped craft hovered over the highway and that he could not account for about 20 minutes. Under later hypnosis he described humanoid beings with a slightly reptilian look and a 'winged serpent' emblem. The University of Colorado UFO study found no evidence the object was physically real; skeptics consider it a hoax.
reptilians|Herbert Schirmer encounter.source_title: Condon Report, Case 42: State Trooper Sighting (NCAS archive)

ropen|First Western expedition.note: Could not verify a 1994 'first Western expedition' in any reliable source. Creationist ropen sites say Americans explored Umboi intermittently from 1994, but no reliable outlet names who went or what happened. Suggest dropping this case or folding it into the 2004 entry.

ropen|Two Umboi Island expeditions.summary: In 2004 two small American teams, including Jonathan Whitcomb, searched Umboi Island in Papua New Guinea for the ropen, said to be a glowing, long-tailed flying creature. They interviewed local witnesses but obtained no video. The searchers were mostly young-earth creationists hoping to show pterosaurs survive; scientists consider the ropen unproven.
ropen|Two Umboi Island expeditions.source_title: The Truth is Out There: On the Wild and Divisive World of Cryptozoology - Literary Hub

rougarou|Rougarou Fest.summary: The first Rougarou Fest was held in downtown Houma on October 26, 2012, mixing Cajun monster lore with a parade, costume contest and a monster-themed run. Proceeds went to the Wetlands Discovery Center, which teaches children about Louisiana's wetlands and coast. The festival has continued as an annual Halloween event.
rougarou|Rougarou Fest.source_title: First Rougarou Fest set for Houma - WWNO

rusalka|Dvořák's opera Rusalka premieres.summary: Antonín Dvořák's opera Rusalka, about a water nymph who falls in love with a human prince, premiered in Prague on March 31, 1901. Jaroslav Kvapil's libretto drew on Czech fairy tales. It became Dvořák's most successful opera and is still widely performed.

sea-monk|Sea monk caught in the Øresund.summary: In about 1546 a creature said to look like a monk in his habit was caught or stranded in the Øresund strait between Denmark and Sweden. King Christian III sent a picture of it to Emperor Charles V, and it appeared in natural histories of the time. In the 1850s zoologist Japetus Steenstrup suggested it was a giant squid; others have proposed a walrus.

sea-serpent|Gloucester Harbor sightings.summary: In August 1817 many people in and around Gloucester Harbor, Massachusetts, including fishermen and the crew of the schooner Caravan, reported a huge serpent-like creature with humps along its back. The Linnaean Society of New England collected sworn statements. Sightings continued into 1819, and the cause has never been settled.

sea-serpent|HMS Daedalus sighting.summary: On August 6, 1848, Captain Peter M'Quhae and officers of the frigate HMS Daedalus reported a 60-ft sea serpent between the Cape of Good Hope and St Helena, which stayed in view for about 20 minutes. The report in The Times caused a long debate. It has never been explained; a 2023 study suggested a harpooned whale towing a capsized boat.

sea-serpent|Valhalla sighting.summary: On December 7, 1905, naturalists Edmund Meade-Waldo and Michael Nicoll, sailing on the Earl of Crawford's yacht Valhalla, saw a large frill or fin about six feet long break the surface, followed by a long neck rising in front of it. The respected witnesses made it one of the most cited sea serpent reports; the animal was never identified.

selkie|Kópakonan seal-woman statue unvei.summary: In 2014 a large bronze statue of Kópakonan, the 'Seal Woman', by Faroese sculptor Hans Pauli Olsen was placed on the shore at Mikladalur on Kalsoy, where the surf sometimes washes over it. It marks the best-known Faroese selkie legend, set in the village, and has become a major tourist attraction.

selma|Oldest written account of the serp.summary: The oldest written account of the Seljord serpent dates from 1750, when it was said to have circled a rowboat crossing Lake Seljord from Ulvenes to Nes. Sightings have tended to peak in hot, calm summers, and the serpent has been on Seljord's coat of arms since 1989.

shadow-people|Coast to Coast AM shadow p.summary: On April 12, 2001, Art Bell's late-night radio show Coast to Coast AM discussed shadow people at length, and listeners were invited to send in drawings of the dark figures they had seen, which were posted online. The show is credited with popularising the idea. Researchers link many such experiences to sleep paralysis.

sharlie|Tie cutters see a 'log' start to.summary: The first documented settler sighting of a creature in Payette Lake dates to 1920, when workers cutting railroad ties at the upper end of the lake saw what they took for a log begin to move. Earlier Native American belief held that an evil spirit lived in the lake.

sharlie|About twenty people watch a 30 t.summary: In September 1946 a group of about twenty people reported seeing the Payette Lake serpent. A doctor from Nampa told the local paper it seemed to be 30 to 40 ft long, kept diving and left a wake like a small motorboat. The report was never confirmed.

sharlie|Newspaper contest names the serp.summary: In 1954 The Star News in McCall held a contest to name the Payette Lake serpent. The winning name, 'Sharlie', came from a reader in Virginia, a nod to the old radio catchphrase 'Vas you dere, Sharlie?'. Sightings were reported on and off until 1997.

sheepsquatch|\"The White Thing\" folk ta.summary: Folklorist Ruth Ann Musick published the tale of the 'White Thing', a shaggy white beast that menaced travellers, in her 1965 book The Telltale Lilac Bush and Other West Virginia Ghost Tales. A Fairmont State student had submitted it in 1954, saying it was common in Kanawha County. It is often seen as an ancestor of the Sheepsquatch.
sheepsquatch|\"The White Thing\" folk ta.source_title: Tale of Kanawha County monster may have first been documented in 1950s - West Virginia Explorer

sheepsquatch|Mid-1990s wave of sightings.note: No reliable source found. Mid-1990s Boone/Kanawha County, WV sightings appear only in blogs and a Mountain Monsters TV episode review; no contemporary newspaper coverage located.

shunka-warakin|Hutchins shoots the anima.summary: In 1886 settler Israel Ammon Hutchins shot a dark, wolf-like animal that had been raiding livestock on his Madison Valley ranch, on what is now the Sun Ranch. He traded the body to Joseph Sherwood, a taxidermist who displayed it as a 'ringdocus' in his store-museum at Henry's Lake, Idaho. Its identity remains uncertain.
shunka-warakin|Hutchins shoots the anima.source_title: Mystery monster returns home after 121 years - Bozeman Daily Chronicle

shunka-warakin|Mount rediscovered and di.summary: In 2007 Jack Kirby, a grandson of Israel Hutchins, traced the long-lost mount to storage at the Idaho Museum of Natural History in Pocatello. The museum loaned it to the Madison Valley History Museum in Ennis, Montana, where it is on display and remains unidentified.
shunka-warakin|Mount rediscovered and di.source_title: Mystery monster returns home after 121 years - Bozeman Daily Chronicle

skinwalker|Book Hunt for the Skinwalker.summary: In 2005 Colm Kelleher and journalist George Knapp published Hunt for the Skinwalker about the Utah ranch bought by Robert Bigelow, popularising the 'Skinwalker Ranch' name, which borrows a name from Navajo tradition. The book described UFOs, cattle deaths and strange creatures; skeptics say years of monitoring found no proof.

skinwalker-ranch|Sherman family story pu.summary: In 1996 the Deseret News in Salt Lake City published the Sherman family's claims of strange events on their ranch near Ballard, including mutilated cattle, lights and unusual creatures. Journalist George Knapp later expanded on them. Skeptic Robert Sheaffer notes that earlier owners reported nothing unusual in 60 years.

skinwalker-ranch|Bigelow buys the ranch.summary: Businessman Robert Bigelow bought the ranch for about $200,000 in 1996 and used it as a monitoring site for his National Institute for Discovery Science. Researchers said they logged many odd incidents but found no proof. James Randi gave Bigelow a mock Pigasus Award, and Bigelow sold the property in 2016.

skinwalker-ranch|Hunt for the Skinwalker.summary: Colm Kelleher and George Knapp's 2005 book Hunt for the Skinwalker described alleged UFOs, Bigfoot-like creatures and poltergeist activity at the ranch. It later prompted a Defense Intelligence Agency official to visit, which helped lead to a $22 million Pentagon study of unidentified aerial phenomena.

skunk-ape|Myakka photographs.summary: In 2000 the Sarasota County Sheriff's Office received two anonymous photos of a large, hairy, ape-like animal. An unsigned letter said they were taken by an elderly woman who feared an escaped orangutan was stealing apples from her porch near I-75. The sender was never identified, and mainstream scientists regard skunk ape evidence as folklore, misidentification or hoax.

snallygaster|Newspaper sightings wave.summary: In February and March 1909 local newspapers reported a winged monster with a long pointed bill, steel-hook claws and one eye, screeching like a locomotive around the Middletown Valley. It was later revealed as a hoax by Middletown Valley Register editor George C. Rhoderick and reporter Ralph S. Wolfe to boost readership, drawing on old German settler folklore.

snallygaster|Second wave of reports.summary: In late 1932 Maryland papers reported the snallygaster was back, seen by 'two score' residents of Washington, Frederick and Montgomery counties. In December the Hagerstown Morning Herald said it had drowned in a moonshine vat in Frog Hollow. The Library of Congress notes some of this coverage used the legend to intimidate Black voters.
snallygaster|Second wave of reports.source_title: American Cryptids - Headlines and Heroes (Library of Congress blog)

snarly-yow|Dahlgren publishes South-Moun.summary: In 1882 Madeleine Vinton Dahlgren published South-Mountain Magic, tales gathered from neighbours after she bought the old South Mountain Inn at Turner's Gap, Maryland. They include the Snarly Yow, a black dog said to haunt the National Road at night that could not be struck or shot.
snarly-yow|Dahlgren publishes South-Moun.source_title: South Mountain, MD: Legends, Civil War History, & Rye Whiskey - Visit Frederick

spriggans|Robert Hunt links spriggans to.summary: Folklorist Robert Hunt's Popular Romances of the West of England (1865) recorded Cornish tales of spriggans, small but immensely strong fairy guardians of buried treasure that could swell to giant size. Hunt tied them especially to Trencrom Hill, a Neolithic hilltop enclosure reused as an Iron Age hillfort.

spriggans|Spriggan sculpture installed o.summary: In 1993 a man-sized green spriggan sculpture by artist Marilyn Collins was placed in an alcove of the old railway arches on London's Parkland Walk, near the former Crouch End station. It is often wrongly linked to Stephen King's story 'Crouch End', which was written years earlier.

spring-heeled-jack|First reported attack.summary: In 1837 stories spread in south-west London of a leaping figure with claw-like hands who attacked people at night, with later accounts placing one attack on Clapham Common. In January 1838 the Lord Mayor of London publicly read a complaint about the scares. No attacker was ever identified.

spring-heeled-jack|Jane Alsop attack.summary: Jane Alsop said that on February 19, 1838 a cloaked man at her father's door in Bow claimed to be a policeman, then breathed blue and white flame at her and tore her dress with metal-like claws. The Times covered the case. A local man who boasted he was Spring-heeled Jack was tried but not convicted.

spring-heeled-jack|Liverpool sightings.summary: Late reports moved Spring-heeled Jack to north-west England. Around 1888 he was said to appear on the roof of St Francis Xavier's Church in Everton, and in 1904 there were reported appearances in nearby William Henry Street, often cited as the last sightings. None were confirmed.

stellers-sea-ape|Georg Steller watches t.summary: On August 10, 1741, near the Shumagin Islands, naturalist Georg Steller of Bering's expedition watched a playful, dog-headed, whiskered animal about 5 ft long for two hours. He tried to shoot it and missed. Later zoologists think he saw a young northern fur seal.

stellers-sea-ape|Miles Smeeton reports a.summary: In June 1965 sailor and author Miles Smeeton said that he and companions on his ketch Tzu Hang saw a 5-ft animal with reddish-yellow fur and a face like a Shih Tzu off the north coast of Atka Island. In a later book he compared it to Steller's description. It was never identified.

storsjoodjuret|First written account.summary: A 1635 manuscript by Morten Pedersen Herdal is the earliest written mention of a serpent in Storsjön. It said the rune-master Kettil Runske had bound the creature to the lake bottom with a spell carved on the Frösö Runestone. Later folk tales described a cat-headed creature with a black serpent body.

storsjoodjuret|Royal-backed capture atte.summary: After a run of sightings, locals formed a company in 1894 to catch the Storsjön creature, with sponsorship from King Oscar II. Traps and hooks caught nothing, and the effort was mocked in a cartoon by Albert Engström in the magazine Strix.

storsjoodjuret|Underwater camera claim.summary: In August 2008 a film crew claimed its underwater infrared cameras in Storsjön had recorded a warm-bodied mass that could be the creature. The footage was not independently confirmed and no animal was identified.

stronsay-beast|Stronsay Beast washes ash.summary: After a storm on September 25, 1808, a carcass measured at about 55 ft washed ashore on Stronsay in Orkney. Edinburgh's Wernerian Society named it a new sea serpent, Halsydrus pontoppidani. Anatomist Everard Home, and later John Goodsir, concluded it was a decomposed basking shark, which can look serpent-like when it rots.

tahoe-tessie|Coggin serpent report.summary: In 1865 a San Francisco visitor named I. C. Coggin reported seeing a massive serpent in Lake Tahoe, with a head 14 ft wide and a body over 600 ft long. It is one of the earliest accounts linked to Tahoe Tessie, and the size claims are generally regarded as exaggerated.

tahoe-tessie|V-shaped wake report.summary: In 2005 a longtime Lake Tahoe fisherman and former sheriff's officer described a large V-shaped wave cutting across the calm lake that he said was not made by any fish or boat. Around the same time visitors reported a dark, humped shape off Tahoe Park Beach. No photos were taken.

tantanoola-tiger|Thomas Donovan shoots t.summary: After reports of a 'tiger' stalking the Tantanoola district, Thomas Donovan shot the culprit in August 1895. It turned out to be a wolf, later identified as an Arabian wolf, though how it reached South Australia is unknown. The stuffed animal is displayed at the Tantanoola Hotel.

tatzelwurm|Balkin photograph.summary: A photographer named Balkin said he photographed a Tatzelwurm by a log in the Aare Gorge near Meiringen, and the image ran in the Berliner Illustrierte, which offered a 1,000-Reichsmark reward. Searchers found nothing, and the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (April 1935) dismissed it as a tourism stunt; many consider it a hoax. Sources date it 1934 or 1935.

thetis-lake-monster|Teenagers chased fro.summary: On August 22, 1972, the Victoria Daily Times reported that two teenage boys said a silvery, scaled creature with claws and a spiked head came out of Thetis Lake. The RCMP found no evidence. Writer Daniel Loxton later found it matched a gill-man film shown on local TV days earlier, and one witness admitted they made it up.

thunderbird|Lawndale incident.summary: On the evening of July 25, 1977, a Lawndale, Illinois family said two huge black birds swooped into their yard and one briefly lifted a young boy off the ground before dropping him. Suggested explanations include a large vulture or a stray condor; nothing was confirmed.
thunderbird|Lawndale incident.source_title: The Mythic Child-Stealing Thunderbirds of Illinois - Atlas Obscura

thylacine|Last known thylacine dies.summary: The last known captive thylacine died at Hobart's Beaumaris Zoo on September 7, 1936, just 59 days after the species was given legal protection. The name 'Benjamin', often given to it, was invented decades later. The thylacine was declared extinct in the 1980s, and September 7 is Australia's National Threatened Species Day.

thylacine|Hans Naarding spotlight sighti.summary: In 1982 Tasmanian Parks and Wildlife ranger Hans Naarding reported seeing a thylacine. His report led to a confidential two-year government search that found no evidence of surviving thylacines.

thylacine|The Bulletin $1.25 million rew.summary: In March 2005 the Australian news magazine The Bulletin offered a $1.25 million reward for the safe capture of a live thylacine as part of its 125th anniversary. When the offer closed at the end of June 2005, no one had produced any evidence.

trunko|Trunko seen fighting killer whale.summary: In October 1924 witnesses at Margate, South Africa said a huge white, furry creature fought two killer whales offshore for hours; a 47-ft carcass with a trunk-like appendage later washed up. The story reached London's Daily Mail in December. Photos found in 2010 led palaeontologist Darren Naish to conclude it was a rotting whale carcass, or globster.

tsuchinoko|Shimokitayama Tsuchinoko Expe.summary: In 1988 Shimokitayama village councillor Kazuo Nozaki launched a 'Tsuchinoko Expedition', offering 1 million yen for a live tsuchinoko, a fat-bodied snake of Japanese folklore. About 200 people from across Japan took part until 1990, but no evidence was found.

tsuchinoko|Tsuchinoko Park opens.summary: In 2023 Shimokitayama in Nara Prefecture opened the Shimokitayama Tsuchinoko Park to commemorate the village's 1988-1990 tsuchinoko hunt. The creature has never been confirmed to exist.

tylwyth-teg|Lady of Llyn y Fan Fach lege.summary: The 1861 book Meddygon Myddvai printed the legend of the Lady of Llyn y Fan Fach, a fairy woman who rose from the lake to marry a local farmer and returned to it after he struck her three times. Her sons were said to become the Physicians of Myddfai. The version was based on oral accounts collected in 1841.

ufo-boomerang|Lubbock Lights.summary: In August and September 1951, three Texas Tech professors and many others in Lubbock reported formations of glowing lights passing overhead, and a student, Carl Hart Jr., photographed a V-shaped group. The Air Force investigated. Project Blue Book's Edward Ruppelt concluded they were probably plovers reflecting the city's new street lights, though the Hart photos were never fully explained.

ufo-boomerang|Hudson Valley boomerang wa.summary: From March 1983 into 1984, thousands of people in Westchester, Putnam and Dutchess counties and western Connecticut reported huge, silent V- or boomerang-shaped formations of lights. State police and the New York Power Authority said the 'UFO' was a group of small Cessna planes flying in tight formation from Stormville Airport as a prank.

ufo-boomerang|Phoenix Lights.summary: On March 13, 1997, people across Arizona reported a huge V- or carpenter's-square-shaped formation of lights, and later a row of hovering lights over Phoenix. The formation was A-10 jets from Operation Snowbird flying back to Tucson, and the later lights were military flares dropped on a range south-west of the city. Governor Fife Symington later said he saw something 'otherworldly'.

ufo-cigar|Chiles-Whitted encounter.summary: At about 2:45 a.m. on July 24, 1948, Eastern Air Lines pilots Clarence Chiles and John Whitted said a glowing, cigar-shaped object with rows of lit windows shot past their DC-3 near Montgomery, Alabama, then pulled up into the clouds. Project Sign took it very seriously, but later Air Force and civilian analysis concluded they saw a bright meteor.

ufo-crash|Roswell debris recovery.summary: In summer 1947 a rancher found metallic and rubber debris on land near Roswell, and Roswell Army Air Field briefly announced it had recovered a 'flying disc' before calling it a weather balloon. The debris was actually from a secret Project Mogul balloon train for detecting Soviet nuclear tests. Alien-crash claims took off only after 1978.

ufo-crash|Kecksburg fireball.summary: On December 9, 1965, a bright fireball was seen over several US states and Ontario, and residents of Kecksburg, Pennsylvania said something came down in nearby woods and later accounts claimed the military removed an acorn-shaped object. Astronomers say it was a meteor, and NASA said in 2005 that fragments examined were from a Soviet satellite, though it had lost the records.

ufo-crash|Shag Harbour impact.summary: On the night of October 4, 1967, witnesses including RCMP officers saw a lit object descend into the water off Shag Harbour, Nova Scotia, where it floated and then sank. Local fishing boats and the Coast Guard searched but found no wreckage. No aircraft were missing, and Canadian government documents list it as an unidentified flying object.

ufo-orbs|Foo fighters.summary: From November 1944, Allied aircrews over Europe and later the Pacific reported glowing balls of light that seemed to pace their planes. The US 415th Night Fighter Squadron named them 'foo fighters', and crews assumed they were enemy secret weapons. The postwar Robertson Panel suggested electrostatic effects like St. Elmo's fire or reflections from ice crystals.

ufo-orbs|Marfa lights.summary: The first recorded account of the Marfa lights dates to 1883, when cowhand Robert Reed Ellison saw a flickering light near Paisano Pass and wondered if it was an Apache campfire. The lights are still seen from a viewing area east of Marfa. Scientists who studied them between 2000 and 2008 concluded most are car headlights distorted by warm desert air.

ufo-saucer|Kenneth Arnold sighting.summary: On June 24, 1947, private pilot Kenneth Arnold reported nine shiny objects flying in a line past Mount Rainier at what he estimated was over 1,200 mph. His description of how they moved led the press to coin the terms 'flying saucer' and 'flying disc', starting the modern UFO era. The Army Air Forces put it down to a mirage; others suggest pelicans.

ufo-saucer|Roswell incident.summary: In July 1947 Roswell Army Air Field announced it had recovered a 'flying disc' from a ranch, then within a day said it was a weather balloon. The material came from Project Mogul, a top-secret balloon program. In 1978 former officer Jesse Marcel claimed a cover-up, and the story grew into claims of alien bodies that have no factual basis.

ufo-saucer|McMinnville photos.summary: On May 11, 1950, Evelyn and Paul Trent took two photos of a saucer-shaped object over their farm near McMinnville, Oregon. Life magazine reprinted them and they became some of the most famous UFO photos. The Condon Committee found the Trents sincere, but most experts consider them a hoax, probably a small model hung from overhead wires; some ufologists disagree.

ufo-tic-tac|Nimitz encounter.summary: On November 14, 2004, Commander David Fravor and other Navy aviators from the USS Nimitz group, sent to check radar contacts off southern California, said they saw a white, oval 'Tic Tac' object over a disturbance in the sea that rose and vanished. A later jet recorded it on infrared (the 'FLIR' video). The Pentagon still lists it as unidentified.

ufo-tic-tac|Gimbal and GoFast videos.summary: In 2014-15, Navy pilots from the USS Theodore Roosevelt group, including Lt. Ryan Graves, recorded the 'Gimbal' and 'GoFast' infrared videos of unidentified objects off the US East Coast. The New York Times published them in 2017. Skeptics such as Mick West argue they show camera artefacts, glare and parallax effects; the Pentagon calls them unidentified.

ufo-triangle|Belgian UFO wave.summary: From November 1989 to April 1990, many Belgians reported large black triangles with bright lights. On the night of March 30-31, 1990 two F-16s were scrambled after radar contacts but never saw anything; skeptics attribute the radar locks to interference. The most famous photo of a triangle was admitted as a hoax in 2011 by the man who made it.

ufo-triangle|Phoenix Lights.summary: On March 13, 1997, thousands across Arizona reported a vast triangular or V-shaped formation of lights passing overhead, followed by a line of hovering lights over Phoenix. Investigators identified the first as A-10 aircraft from Operation Snowbird and the second as illumination flares dropped on the Barry Goldwater Range.

van-meter-visitor|Five nights of sightin.summary: In 1903 newspapers reported that residents of Van Meter, Iowa saw a winged, bat-like creature over several nights, said to shine a light from a horn on its forehead and to be unharmed by bullets. The story became a local legend, now marked by an annual Van Meter Visitor Festival.

vegetable-man|Jennings Frederick's claim.summary: Jennings Frederick said that in July 1968, near Grant Town, a thin plant-like creature with yellow eyes asked for help telepathically, then drew blood from his wrist with needle-like fingers before leaping away. The story was first printed in 1976 by Gray Barker, a known hoaxer. There is no physical evidence and no other sighting.

waitoreke|Cook's crew see a cat-sized fo.summary: During James Cook's stay at Dusky Sound on his second voyage, three or four crew members saw a four-footed animal about the size of a cat, with short legs and mouse-coloured fur. Cook noted that no two descriptions matched. Later reports of a New Zealand 'otter' followed, but no specimen has been found; seals and introduced dogs have been suggested.

wampus-cat|Knoxville paper describes a 1.summary: In 1936 The Knoxville News-Sentinel described the wampus cat as having 'a body 15 or 20 feet long, and eyes like small moons'. The wampus cat is a figure of Appalachian folklore, usually pictured as a panther-like creature with glowing eyes and a scream like a cougar.

wendigo|Blackwood's story The Wendigo.summary: English writer Algernon Blackwood published the novella The Wendigo in 1910, popularising the word in English. Its version of the creature differs from the wīhtikōw/wiindigoo of Cree and Ojibwe tradition, a being tied to greed and cannibalism, yet it shaped much later horror fiction.

white-river-monster|First reported sight.summary: Sightings of a large creature in the White River near Newport began in 1915. On July 1 a plantation owner said he saw a grey-skinned animal 'as wide as a car and three cars long'. A plan to catch it with a rope net was dropped for lack of money.

white-river-monster|Bateman sightings an.summary: In 1937 plantation owner Bramlett Bateman said he saw a creature 'with the skin of an elephant', 12 ft long and 4-5 ft wide, in an eddy of the White River. He wanted to blast it with TNT but was refused permission. The story drew visitors from across the country, some with cameras and guns, before sightings stopped.

white-river-monster|Boxcar-sized sightin.summary: In summer 1971 witnesses described a peeling-skinned creature 'the size of a boxcar' with a bone on its forehead, and 14-inch three-toed tracks were reported on Towhead Island. Biologist Roy Mackal suggested a stray elephant seal; others point to a very large alligator gar.

white-river-monster|White River Monster.summary: In 1973 the Arkansas legislature passed a bill by state Senator Robert Harvey creating the White River Monster Refuge along a stretch of the river between Old Grand Glaize and Rosie. It is illegal to harm the monster within the refuge.

white-thing|Ruth Ann Musick prints the t.summary: Fairmont State folklorist Ruth Ann Musick printed the tale of the 'White Thing', a shaggy white beast said to menace people in Kanawha County, in her 1965 book The Telltale Lilac Bush and Other West Virginia Ghost Tales. A student had submitted it in 1954, saying it was then common in the county. Musick called such creatures supernatural rather than ghosts.
white-thing|Ruth Ann Musick prints the t.source_title: Tale of Kanawha County monster may have first been documented in 1950s - West Virginia Explorer

wild-man-of-the-navidad|Settlers report.summary: From about 1836, settlers along the Navidad River near present-day Sublime reported food and tools going missing at night, with tools sometimes returned polished. Some described hairy wild people. A historical marker says the 'wild man' was a man who had escaped slavery; he was captured in 1851.
wild-man-of-the-navidad|Settlers report.source_title: Wild Man of the Navidad - Wikipedia

wolfman-of-defiance|Railroad crewman rep.summary: In late July and early August 1972, Defiance police said people near the Norfolk and Western tracks had been accosted at night by a very tall figure 'with some kind of animal head'; one man was hit on the shoulder with a board. More scares followed, but no one was caught and many locals assumed a prankster in a mask.
wolfman-of-defiance|Railroad crewman rep.source_title: Anniversary of 'wolfman' sightings in Defiance - The Crescent-News

yeren|Chinese Academy of Sciences expedi.summary: In 1977, after a rise in reports, Zhou Guoxing led a large Chinese Academy of Sciences expedition into Shennongjia, with soldiers, zoologists and photographers, to look for the yeren or 'wild man'. Later searches followed, but all hair and footprint evidence traced to known animals such as bears and monkeys, and scientific interest faded by the late 1980s.

yeti|Howard-Bury tracks.summary: In 1921 Lt-Col Charles Howard-Bury, leading the British Everest reconnaissance, found tracks crossing the Lhakpa La at about 21,000 ft. He thought a large wolf made them, but his Sherpa guides said they belonged to the 'wild man of the snows'. The name 'Abominable Snowman' was coined that year from a garbled version of the local term.

yeti|Shipton footprint photo.summary: In 1951, on a reconnaissance of Everest, mountaineer Eric Shipton photographed large footprints in the snow on the Menlung Glacier, one beside an ice axe and boot for scale. The photos became the most famous yeti evidence. Skeptics argue melting snow distorted ordinary tracks, and researcher Daniel C. Taylor links them to bears.

yeti|Pangboche hand.summary: Expeditions funded by Tom Slick learned of a 'yeti hand' kept as a relic at Pangboche monastery; in 1959 one member took pieces of it, reportedly replacing them with human bones. Edmund Hillary called it a hoax in 1960, the hand was stolen from the monastery in 1991, and in 2011 DNA tests showed a sampled finger bone was human.

yowie|Kilcoy sightings.summary: Two students camping in bushland near Kilcoy reported meeting a 'two to three-metre brown hairy creature'. Kilcoy embraced the story, putting up a yowie statue, naming Yowie Park and nicknaming its rugby team 'The Yowies'.

yunwi-tsunsdi|James Mooney publishes Myt.summary: In 1900 Smithsonian ethnologist James Mooney published Myths of the Cherokee, based on years of work with Cherokee storytellers in North Carolina. It describes the Yûñwi Tsunsdi', small, kind but easily offended 'Little People' who live in rock caves and help lost travellers. These beings remain part of living Cherokee tradition.
yunwi-tsunsdi|James Mooney publishes Myt.source_title: Myths of the Cherokee by James Mooney - Project Gutenberg

zuiyo-maru-carcass|Trawler Zuiyō Maru ha.summary: On April 25, 1977, the Japanese trawler Zuiyō Maru, fishing east of Christchurch, hauled up a large rotting carcass that some said looked like a plesiosaur. The crew photographed it and threw it back to protect the catch. Tests of tissue samples later pointed to a decomposed basking shark.

ufo-saucer|Falcon Lake incident.summary: Prospector Stefan Michalak said a landed, metallic craft burned his chest when it lifted off. The RCMP, RCAF and Department of National Defence investigated; his burns were real, but his story shifted and later marks were judged self-inflicted. See the full case in Close encounters.

ufo-saucer|Langenburg saucers.summary: Farmer Edwin Fuhr said five spinning saucers hovered a foot above the ground by a slough, then shot away silently. The RCMP found five matching circles and no sign anyone had driven in to make them.

ufo-saucer|Clarenville sighting.summary: Early on October 26, twelve people reported an oval object with a fin hovering over the water near Random Island. RCMP Constable James Blackwood watched it for one to two hours through a surveillance telescope and said it flashed back when he shone his headlights at it. It left no physical evidence.

ufo-orbs|Petrozavodsk phenomenon.summary: Before dawn on September 20, a glowing object seemed to shower the Soviet city of Petrozavodsk with rays, and glowing objects were reported from Helsinki and Copenhagen to Vladivostok. It is often, though not universally, put down to the launch of the Kosmos-955 satellite. A Soviet Academy of Sciences report could not explain it, and the event helped start Setka, the Soviet research programme on anomalous phenomena.

ufo-orbs|Bonaventure Hotel lights.summary: On November 7, people at the rooftop pool of Montreal's Bonaventure Hotel watched 8 to 10 lights form a circle overhead and shine bright white rays for about three hours. La Presse and the CBC covered it, and no one identified the lights.

dungarvon-whooper|Whelan's ballad publis.summary: In 1912 the New Brunswick poet Michael Whelan published a ballad telling the story as lumbermen knew it. A young cook was left alone in a Dungarvon River lumber camp with the camp boss, who killed him for the money in his belt. The men buried him in the woods, and that night a terrible whooping drove them from the camp. Only a priest's prayers at the grave settled it. Some have suggested the cry was a screech owl or a cougar.

alyoshenka|Body found near the village c.summary: In mid-1996 Tamara Prosvirina, 74, of Kaolinovy near Kyshtym in Russia's Chelyabinsk region, found a tiny mummified body near the village cemetery. She took it home, called it Alyoshenka and cared for it as if it were alive. After she was taken to hospital, neighbours gave the body to the police, who opened an investigation. A local gynecologist examined it and concluded it was a premature fetus.

alyoshenka|DNA test identifies a prematu.summary: A DNA test was carried out later, and it strongly supported the first finding: the remains were a prematurely born human baby with birth defects. A little doubt lingered only because the original body had been lost by then, so the test could not be repeated on it. Only photos and video survive.

cressie|The Parsons sighting.summary: On July 9, 1991, Fred Parsons and his wife reported a large, snake-like animal swimming in Crescent Lake. He said it had a long, sleek body without a noticeably large head, lying level with the water.

cressie|A rolling black shape.summary: In September 1991 a Robert's Arm man driving back into town saw the lake's surface churn. A black shape about 15 feet long rose and pitched forward in a rolling motion, like a whale but with no fin, then sank and did not come back.

cressie|Summer of sightings.summary: In summer 2003, after a year or more with no reports, several residents said they saw the creature again: a snake-like animal with a fish-like head, its skin shiny in the sun. One passenger said she watched water pour from its open mouth as it crossed the lake.

mugwump|A couple see it swimming.summary: In 1978 a married couple said they watched the creature swimming in Lake Timiskaming. They described a humped back with no fins and put its length at no less than 15 feet.

mugwump|The mayor's newspaper story.summary: On April 20, 1979, New Liskeard mayor Jack Dent wrote in the North Bay Nugget that an unnamed source had told him of an old Algonquin story about a creature 'the length of four Indian braves' living in the lake. Weeks later The Temiskaming Speaker printed Chuck Coull's account of an encounter in the early 1960s, and local interest took off.

mugwump|Ice fishers meet its eye.summary: In 1982 two ice fishers said a black, glistening head rose in their fishing hole. It had protruding eyes, and one of them seemed to be sizing the men up.

pend-oreille-paddler|First reports from.summary: The first reports of a large, unknown shape in Lake Pend Oreille date from 1944, while the Farragut Naval Training Station was running on the lake's southern shore. Many locals have long suspected the Navy's later submarine testing in the deep lake explains the sightings.

pend-oreille-paddler|The papier-mâché ca.summary: In late 1984 a professor's cryptozoology club tracked down the tabloid photo of the 'Paddler'. It showed a 12-foot papier-mâché catfish built for a 1974 play in Sandpoint. The name stuck anyway.

pend-oreille-paddler|A teacher chases a.summary: On Memorial Day 1985 Julie Green, a Coeur d'Alene teacher, said she saw a 'gunmetal grey object' a few hundred yards from her boat and gave chase. Some took her description as support for the theory that the Navy used the monster to cover its submarine tests.

walgren-lake-monster|Old Jules mentions.summary: In Old Jules, her 1935 biography of her father, Nebraska writer Mari Sandoz recalled how famous the monster had become, and that some local churchgoers said the devil had planted it to test the faithful.

walgren-lake-monster|The tall-tale versi.summary: In July 1938 the Federal Writers' Project's Nebraska Tall Tales described the monster as so huge that the earth shook when it moved, leaving farmers seasick for miles, and said it came ashore every day to eat livestock and breathe out a thick green mist.

fur-bearing-trout|A shaggy trout washes.summary: In 1854 a 'shaggy trout' was reported cast ashore at Svínavatn in northern Iceland. An Icelandic newspaper printed an illustration the next year showing reddish hair on its jaw, neck, sides and fins.

fur-bearing-trout|Montana Wildlife print.summary: In 1929 Montana Wildlife magazine ran an article by J.H. Hicken about trout that had grown fur, the earliest known American printing of the tall tale.
